text: Name the seven layers of the OSI model and state the unit of data at each.
expectedAnswerPoints: Physical (bits), Data Link (frames), Network (packets), Transport (segments), Session, Presentation, Application
Physical handles raw bit transmission over the medium
Data Link handles framing, MAC addressing and error/flow control on a single link
Network handles logical addressing and routing between networks
Transport handles process-to-process delivery, reliability and congestion control
Session manages dialogs, Presentation handles translation/encryption/compression, Application is the user interface

text: What is the difference between a hub, a switch and a router?
expectedAnswerPoints: A hub works at the physical layer and simply broadcasts incoming data to all connected ports
A switch works at the data link layer and forwards frames only to the correct port using MAC addresses
A router works at the network layer and forwards packets between different networks using IP addresses and a routing table
A hub creates one shared collision domain; a switch gives each port its own collision domain
A switch reduces unnecessary traffic; a router additionally separates broadcast domains

text: Explain circuit switching, message switching and packet switching, and where each is used.
expectedAnswerPoints: Circuit switching reserves a dedicated path for the whole duration of the communication, as in traditional telephone networks
Circuit switching is reliable with fixed delay but wastes capacity when the link is idle
Message switching stores and forwards a complete message at each node, suitable for non-real-time data like email
Packet switching splits data into independently routed packets, used by the internet
Packet switching uses bandwidth efficiently and handles bursty traffic well, but packets may be delayed, lost or arrive out of order

text: Compare the datagram approach and the virtual circuit approach in packet switching.
expectedAnswerPoints: Datagram is connectionless: no path is set up beforehand and each packet is routed independently
Virtual circuit is connection-oriented: a path is established before data transfer and all packets follow it
Datagram packets carry the full destination address, giving higher per-packet overhead
Virtual circuit packets carry a short circuit identifier instead, lowering overhead
Datagram packets may arrive out of order or be lost; virtual circuit packets arrive in order and more reliably
IP uses the datagram approach; ATM and Frame Relay use virtual circuits

text: What is the difference between flow control and congestion control?
expectedAnswerPoints: Flow control prevents a fast sender from overwhelming a slow receiver
Flow control is an end-to-end concern based on the receiver's buffer/window size
Congestion control prevents senders from overwhelming the network itself
Congestion control responds to conditions inside the network, such as router queue buildup and packet loss
TCP implements flow control via the advertised receive window and congestion control via slow start, congestion avoidance, fast retransmit and fast recovery

text: Explain the Stop-and-Wait, Go-Back-N and Selective Repeat protocols.
expectedAnswerPoints: Stop-and-Wait sends one frame and waits for its acknowledgement before sending the next; window size is 1
Stop-and-Wait is simple but inefficient because the sender is idle while waiting
Go-Back-N allows N unacknowledged frames in flight and uses cumulative acknowledgements
On error, Go-Back-N retransmits the lost frame and every frame after it, even correctly received ones
Selective Repeat retransmits only the specific lost or damaged frames and buffers out-of-order frames at the receiver
Selective Repeat is more efficient but requires more buffering and more complex bookkeeping

text: How does CRC differ from a simple checksum for error detection?
expectedAnswerPoints: A checksum computes a sum-based value over the data, transmits it, and the receiver recomputes and compares
CRC treats the data as a polynomial and uses polynomial division to produce a remainder as the check value
CRC is substantially more robust, particularly at detecting burst errors
Checksums are cheaper to compute and are used in TCP/UDP/IP headers
CRC is used at the data link layer, for example in the Ethernet frame trailer, and in storage systems
Both detect errors only; neither corrects them

text: Explain CSMA/CD and CSMA/CA, and why wireless networks use CA rather than CD.
expectedAnswerPoints: Both sense the medium before transmitting to reduce collisions
CSMA/CD detects collisions during transmission, sends a jam signal, then backs off for a random time and retries
CSMA/CA tries to avoid collisions using an interframe space and a random backoff within a contention window before transmitting
CSMA/CA relies on acknowledgements, since a sender assumes collision if no ACK arrives
Wireless cannot reliably detect collisions because a station cannot listen while transmitting and because of the hidden terminal problem
CSMA/CD is used in legacy shared Ethernet; CSMA/CA is used in Wi-Fi

text: What is subnetting and why is it useful?
expectedAnswerPoints: Subnetting divides a large network into smaller logical networks called subnets
Bits are borrowed from the host portion to create the subnet portion
Number of subnets is 2 raised to the borrowed bits; usable hosts per subnet is 2 raised to the remaining host bits, minus 2
Two addresses are reserved per subnet: the network ID (all host bits 0) and the broadcast address (all host bits 1)
Benefits include more efficient IP allocation, reduced broadcast traffic and congestion, and better security through isolation

text: What are the main differences between IPv4 and IPv6?
expectedAnswerPoints: IPv4 uses 32-bit addresses, IPv6 uses 128-bit addresses, solving address exhaustion
IPv4 has a variable header of 20 to 60 bytes; IPv6 has a fixed 40-byte header
IPv6 removes the header checksum to speed up router processing
IPv6 replaces the IPv4 options field with separate extension headers
In IPv6 fragmentation is done only by the source, not by intermediate routers
IPv6 renames TTL to Hop Limit and adds a Flow Label field for flow identification

text: What is ARP and what problem does it solve?
expectedAnswerPoints: Address Resolution Protocol maps a known IP address to the corresponding MAC address on a local network
It is needed because delivery on a LAN happens using MAC addresses, not IP addresses
The sender first checks its ARP cache for the mapping
If absent, it broadcasts an ARP request asking who owns that IP
The device with that IP replies with its MAC address, which the sender caches for future use

text: What is NAT and why is it needed?
expectedAnswerPoints: Network Address Translation lets many devices with private IP addresses share one public IP address
It exists because the IPv4 address space is limited and cannot give every device a public address
It runs on a router or firewall at the network boundary
It rewrites IP addresses and port numbers, tracking mappings in a NAT table
It also provides incidental security by hiding the internal network structure from outside

text: Explain the TCP connection termination process.
expectedAnswerPoints: Termination normally takes four steps because the connection is full duplex and each direction closes independently
The client sends FIN to indicate it has no more data to send
The server acknowledges with ACK, at which point the connection is half-closed
The server may continue sending data, then sends its own FIN when ready
The client sends a final ACK and the connection is fully closed
A three-way variant occurs when the server combines its ACK and FIN into one segment

text: Explain what happens, step by step, when you type a URL into a browser and press Enter.
expectedAnswerPoints: The browser checks its cache, then the OS resolver and local DNS cache, for the domain's IP address
If not cached, a DNS query is resolved via the root server, the TLD server and finally the authoritative name server
ARP resolves the MAC address of the default gateway for the first hop
A TCP connection is established with the server using the three-way handshake, and TLS is negotiated for HTTPS
The browser sends an HTTP GET request and the server responds with the resource
The browser parses the HTML and issues further requests for referenced assets, then renders the page

text: What are the four types of network delay, and which of them is affected by congestion?
expectedAnswerPoints: Transmission delay: time to push all bits of the packet onto the link, equal to packet size divided by bandwidth
Propagation delay: time for a bit to travel across the medium, equal to distance divided by propagation velocity
Queueing delay: time the packet waits in a router's buffer before being processed
Processing delay: time the router takes to examine the header and decide where to forward
Queueing delay is the one most affected by congestion, and it has no fixed formula because it depends on live traffic
Total nodal delay is the sum of all four
